hints: Add one row at a time: 4 + 4 + 4.

teach.heading: Groups that match
teach.body:
A group is a little pile. When every pile is the same size, you can add the same number again and again to find the total.

If 3 dancers each hold 4 pom-poms, that is 4 and 4 and 4.

teach.heading: They have to be equal
teach.body:
This only works if every group is the same size.

If one girl has 4 ribbons, one has 7, and one has 2, the piles do not match. You just have to add them the long way.

teach.heading: Say it out loud
teach.body:
Say "3 groups of 4." Saying it helps you picture it.

Then count the groups one at a time. Do not rush.

practice.prompt: One dancer has 3 bows. One has 6 bows. One has 1 bow.
practice.question: Are these equal groups?
choices: No, the piles are different sizes
practice.correct: No, the piles are different sizes
practice.explain: 3, 6 and 1 do not match. Equal groups all have to be the same size.

practice.question: How many groups of 4 is that?
practice.explain: Count the 4s. There are three of them. 3 groups of 4.

practice.question: What does she mean?
practice.explain: 2 groups of 5 means a 5 and another 5. That is 10.

reinforce.prompt: A pile has 2. Another has 2. Another has 9.
reinforce.question: Are these equal groups?
reinforce.explain: 9 does not match the 2s, so the groups are not equal.

reinforce.question: How many groups of 2?
reinforce.explain: Count the 2s. There are four. 4 groups of 2 makes 8.

walk.setup:
3 dancers are getting ready.
Each dancer holds 4 ribbons. 🎀

steps.say: Let's look at just ONE dancer first.
steps.ask: How many ribbons does one dancer hold?
hints: Look at the box on the left. Count what is inside it.
Point at each ribbon and say a number: 1, 2, 3, 4.
There are 4 ribbons in the box. One dancer holds 4.

steps.say: Now the second dancer comes out. She holds the same amount.
steps.ask: How many ribbons do TWO dancers hold?
hints: Count every ribbon you can see: 1, 2, 3, 4 ... 5, 6, 7, 8.

steps.say: Here comes the third dancer.
steps.ask: How many ribbons altogether?
hints: You had 8. Now there are 4 more.

walk.recap:
3 dancers, 4 ribbons each.
4 + 4 + 4 = 12.
That is 3 groups of 4.

walk.setup:
5 singers line up for the show.
Each one holds 2 song sheets. 📄

steps.say: Start with one singer.
steps.ask: How many sheets does one singer hold?
hints: Count what is in the first box.

steps.say: Two more singers join her. Every singer holds 2.
steps.ask: How many sheets do THREE singers hold?

steps.say: The last two singers come out.
steps.ask: How many sheets do all FIVE singers hold?
hints: You had 6. Two more singers means 2 more, then 2 more.

walk.recap:
5 singers, 2 sheets each.
Jump by 2 five times: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10.

lessons.title: Skip counting
lessons.subtitle: A faster way to count groups.

teach.heading: Jump. Do not crawl.
teach.body:
You do not have to count every single thing one at a time.

You can jump. To count groups of 5, jump by 5.

teach.heading: One jump is one group
teach.body:
Every jump you take is one more group.

Jump by 5 four times and you have counted 4 groups of 5.

teach.heading: Start with the easy jumps
teach.body:
Twos, fives and tens are the easiest to jump.

Learn those three and you can count almost anything fast.

practice.prompt: Start at 0 and jump by 5, four times.
practice.question: Where do you land?
What comes next?
practice.explain: You are jumping by 2. After 8 comes 10.

practice.question: What comes next?
practice.explain: You are jumping by 10. After 30 comes 40.

reinforce.prompt: Jump by 2 five times, starting at 0.
reinforce.question: Where do you land?
What comes next?
reinforce.explain: You are jumping by 5. After 15 comes 20.

reinforce.prompt: Jump by 10 three times, starting at 0.
reinforce.question: Where do you land?

walk.setup:
4 teams walk onto the floor.
There are 5 girls on every team. 👧

steps.say: Look at the first team on its own.
steps.ask: How many girls are on one team?
hints: Count the girls inside the first box.

steps.say: The second team comes out. Instead of counting all over again, JUMP by 5.
steps.ask: You jump by 5 two times. Where do you land?
hints: Start at 5. One more jump of 5.

steps.say: Now all four teams are out. Keep jumping by 5.
steps.ask: How many girls on all four teams?
hints: You are at 10. Two more jumps to go.

walk.recap:
5, 10, 15, 20.
Four teams of 5 is 20 girls.
Jumping is faster than counting every one.

walk.setup:
6 dancers are putting on their shoes.
Every dancer needs 2 shoes. 🩰

steps.say: One dancer first.
steps.ask: How many shoes does one dancer need?

steps.say: Two more dancers sit down. Jump by 2 this time.
steps.ask: Three dancers now. Where does jumping by 2 land you?
hints: Start at 2, then jump twice more.

steps.say: All six dancers are ready.
steps.ask: How many shoes altogether?
hints: You are at 6. Three more dancers to go.

lessons.title: Rows and columns
lessons.subtitle: Lining things up makes it easy.

teach.heading: Every row is a group
teach.body:
When things line up in neat rows, each row is a group.

Count one row. Then add that number again for every other row.

teach.heading: It works both ways
teach.body:
You can count across the rows, or down the columns.

You get the same answer either way. Try it and see.

teach.heading: That is a handy trick
teach.body:
If one way feels hard, turn it around.

2 rows of 5 might be easier than 5 rows of 2. Both give you 10.

practice.prompt: The squad lines up in 3 rows. Each row has 5 girls.
practice.question: How many girls?

practice.prompt: Someone says 2 rows of 5 and 5 rows of 2 give different totals.
practice.question: Are they right?
practice.explain: Turning it around does not change the total. Both make 10.

practice.prompt: You find 5 rows of 2 hard, but you are good at fives.
practice.question: What is the easier way?

reinforce.prompt: Does 4 rows of 3 give the same total as 3 rows of 4?
reinforce.question: Same or different?
reinforce.explain: Rows or columns, you land on 12 either way.

walk.setup:
The squad lines up in 3 rows.
There are 5 girls in every row. ⭐

steps.say: Here is the front row on its own.
steps.ask: How many girls are in one row?
hints: Count along the first row only.

steps.say: The second row lines up behind them. Rows always match.
steps.ask: How many girls are in two rows?

steps.say: And the back row lines up.
steps.ask: How many girls in all three rows?
hints: You are at 10, with one row of 5 to add.
steps.yes: Fifteen. That is the whole squad.

walk.recap:
3 rows with 5 in each.
5, 10, 15. The squad is 15 girls.

walk.setup:
Same girls, new formation.
Now they stand in 5 rows with 3 in each. ⭐

steps.say: Look at the front row of the new shape.
steps.ask: How many girls in one row now?
hints: Three in a row this time.

steps.say: Everybody lines up. Five rows, 3 in each.
steps.ask: How many girls altogether?
hints: Jump by 3, once for each row.

steps.say: 3 rows of 5 was 15. And 5 rows of 3 is also 15.
steps.ask: So what happens when you turn it around?
hints: Look at both answers you worked out.
The first way gave 15. The second way gave 15.
Same girls, same total. Turning it around changes nothing.
steps.yes: Exactly the same. That is a handy trick.

walk.recap:
3 rows of 5 = 15.
5 rows of 3 = 15.
Turn it around and the total stays put.

teach.heading: Sharing fairly
teach.body:
Sharing fairly means everybody ends up with the same amount.

If 12 ribbons are shared by 2 girls, hand them out one at a time until they are gone. Both piles will match.

teach.heading: Nobody gets extra
teach.body:
It is only a fair share if the piles are equal.

One girl cannot take 8 while the other gets 4. That is not sharing.

teach.heading: Check by putting it back
teach.body:
Finished sharing? Add the piles back up.

If you get the number you started with, you did it right.

practice.prompt: 10 medals are shared by 2 gymnasts. Both get the same.
practice.question: How many each?

practice.prompt: 8 girls need to make lines of 2.
practice.question: How many lines?

practice.prompt: 10 candies. One girl takes 7. The other gets 3.
practice.question: Is that a fair share?
choices: No, the piles are not equal
practice.correct: No, the piles are not equal
practice.explain: 7 and 3 do not match. A fair share would be 5 and 5.

reinforce.prompt: 9 stickers. One girl takes 6, the other takes 3.
reinforce.question: Fair share?
reinforce.explain: 6 and 3 do not match, so it is not a fair share.

walk.setup:
There are 12 ribbons in the box.
2 friends want to share them. 🎀

steps.say: Sharing fairly means nobody gets more than anybody else.
steps.ask: If they share fairly, do both girls end up with the same?
hints: Think about what the word fair means.
If one girl got more, would that be fair?
Fair sharing means both piles match.
steps.yes: Right. Both piles have to match.

steps.say: Hand them out one at a time. One for her, one for her, and keep going until the box is empty.
steps.ask: How many ribbons ended up in the first pile?
hints: Count what is in the first box now.

steps.say: The other pile is the same, because you shared fairly.
steps.ask: How many ribbons does each girl get?
hints: Both piles are the same size.

walk.recap:
12 ribbons shared by 2 girls is 6 each.
Check it by adding back: 6 + 6 = 12.

walk.setup:
10 medals to hand out.
5 gymnasts are waiting. 🏅

steps.say: Give the first gymnast her fair share.
steps.ask: How many medals are in the first pile?
hints: Two medals in the first pile.

steps.say: Two more gymnasts get theirs. Everybody gets the same.
steps.ask: How many medals have been handed out now?

steps.say: The last two gymnasts get theirs and the box is empty.
steps.ask: How many medals does each gymnast get?
hints: Every pile is the same size.
steps.yes: Two each, and none left over.

walk.recap:
10 medals shared by 5 gymnasts is 2 each.
Check it: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10.

teach.heading: Pair them up
teach.body:
Take any number of girls and pair them up two by two.

If everybody gets a partner, that number is even. If one is left standing, it is odd.
teach.example: 8 → 4 pairs, nobody left  ·  9 → 4 pairs and 1 left

teach.heading: Even numbers
teach.body:
Even numbers always pair up perfectly.

2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 are even. So is every number you land on when you jump by 2.

teach.heading: Look at the last digit
teach.body:
You do not have to pair up a big number to know.

Just look at the very last digit. If it ends in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8, the number is even.
teach.example: 14 ends in 4 → even  ·  17 ends in 7 → odd

practice.prompt: 7 cheerleaders pair up two by two.
practice.question: Does everybody get a partner?
practice.explain: 7 is odd. Odd numbers always leave one out.

practice.question: Odd or even?
practice.explain: 12 ends in 2, so it is even.

practice.question: How many pairs?
practice.explain: 6 pairs up into 3 twos, with nobody left over.

practice.question: Odd or even?
practice.explain: 15 ends in 5, so it is odd.

reinforce.question: Anyone left over?
reinforce.explain: 10 is even, so it pairs up perfectly.

reinforce.question: Odd or even?
reinforce.explain: 9 ends in 9, so it is odd.

reinforce.question: Odd or even?
reinforce.explain: 20 ends in 0, so it is even.

walk.setup:
8 cheerleaders need a partner each.
They pair up, two by two. 📣

steps.say: Two girls holding hands make one pair.
steps.ask: How many girls are in one pair?
steps.yes: Two. That is what a pair means.

steps.say: Everybody finds somebody. Count the pairs, not the girls.
steps.ask: How many pairs did 8 girls make?
hints: Count the boxes, not what is inside them.

steps.say: Now look carefully at the whole floor.
steps.ask: Was anybody left standing on her own?
hints: Look for a girl who is not in a box.
Count the girls in the pairs: 2, 4, 6, 8. That is all of them.
All 8 girls are in a pair. Nobody is left out.
steps.yes: Nobody left out. That makes 8 an EVEN number.

walk.recap:
8 girls made 4 pairs with nobody left over.
A number that pairs up perfectly is EVEN.

walk.setup:
The next day, 9 cheerleaders come to practice.
They try to pair up again. 📣

steps.say: Here are all the pairs they managed to make.
steps.ask: How many girls are standing in pairs?
hints: Count the girls inside the boxes only.
steps.yes: Eight of them are paired up.

steps.say: But 9 girls came to practice today, not 8.
steps.ask: How many girls could not find a partner?
hints: You started with 9. You paired up 8.
One girl is left standing on her own.

steps.say: 8 pairs up perfectly. 9 leaves one girl out.
steps.ask: So what kind of number is 9?
hints: Even numbers pair up with nobody left over.
A number that leaves somebody out is ODD.
steps.yes: Odd. Nine leaves one out every time.

walk.recap:
9 girls made 4 pairs and left 1 girl over.
A number that leaves one out is ODD.
